utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And despite the outside weather conditions, a very good morning to everybody. And may we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The ordinary question; any protective measures necessary for Witness 71?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no protective measures requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask immediately the usher to escort Mr. Momir Pusac into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, is it possible for the Defence to provide the names or the numbers of the witnesses who are going to be testifying next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll provide the Prosecution, during the break, with the names for the next week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be excellent; also the Chamber would know about the fate of next week.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The request related to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would like to note that the microphone was switched off. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pusac. You can hear me in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have your seat. And the witness is yours, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pusac.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with John Ostojic, I represent the Defence team of Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. I should -- I ought to address you with the title of Dr. Pusac, and not Mr. Pusac, in fact. So that's how we shall continue. I shall be addressing you as Dr. Pusac from now on. Would you be so kind as to give us your name and surname for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Momir Pusac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us your father's name.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Velimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The 11th of March, 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is which municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I'm a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Dr. Pusac, where you completed primary school.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I started in Banja Luka, but unfortunately, because of the earthquake there, I completed my secondary schooling in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to university? If so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I attended the faculty of medicine and graduated from there in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year did you graduate from the faculty of medicine in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After graduation, where did you start working?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: 1979, after I had graduated. I had a stipend. I was a scholarship holder from the health centre Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't give you any leeway, a little break after your studies? You had to start working straight away?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I had a brief holiday of one month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you work in Prijedor before you left for your regular military service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In the autumn. I went to do my military service, regular military service, in September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you do your service for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Until 1980, the 2nd of August, in fact. And then I went back to Prijedor to take up my work there for a certain period of time, and then I worked in the health centre at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you work in Omarska as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Until 1983. I think it was the 18th of April, 1983, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I went to the garrison medical centre in Banja Luka, and I volunteered to work in the first aid department of the military as an active-duty service there. And they took me in for that position. There was a competition, a post was opened, I applied, and they took me in, and I worked in the medical department of the garrison, attached to the garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reasons you decided to go to work for the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't solved my housing problem, and at that time, the army could do a lot more for me in that sense. They could allocate flats, and the possibility for going on to specialisation was greater. I wanted to live in a larger town and ensure a livelihood for myself and my family, a more comfortable life, and everything that I could do for them, especially for my children. And there are far more opportunities in Banja Luka than there were in Prijedor and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work for the army? How long did you stay working there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Until the end of 2001, or rather the 28th of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, how you saw the events that took place in 1992 immediately prior to the month of April of that year.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't even like to recall those days. They were bad days for any normal person, and the mere thought of having to recollect those days, the days that preceded the war, and especially the war days, is a very bad feeling to experience. We lived in a community, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in the town of Prijedor and in my town of Omarska. We would meet each other, we would share the good and the bad. All three ethnic groups, all three nationalities. And at that time, I was not able to differentiate who was a Croat, who was a Muslim. We were all one. They were all my roommates, at university and during my schooling in Sarajevo and Banja Luka, and later on at university, Muslims and Croats alike. I shared good and evil with them. When I say "evil," there was no evil, but I remember the earthquake. That was a natural disaster, and we helped each other when the earthquake struck. Of course, something that happened during that period of communism, the one-party system, especially for us intellectuals, is something that exerted some sort of pressure. It was a sort of burden to us in a way. And we wanted to rid ourselves of that yoke, to live in a multiparty system, in a democracy, in which people would be able to express their views freely and in which they would be able to realise together all the programmes and everything that was progressive. And that is something that happened in the 1990s, in fact. But unfortunately, what I can say now, here and now before this Honourable Tribunal and Trial Chamber, is the following: When we were given the possibility of seizing democracy and freedom, it is my view that we didn't know how to use it properly right out at the start in the proper sense of the word. We weren't able to seize it properly, and already at the very outset, different parties appeared in all three ethnic groups, of course, with their own wishes and desires. They wanted to see a different kind of system. They thought that Yugoslavia was superfluous, that it would be better to live separately, that each republic should be an independent state. And up until that time, we had all lived together, and I personally felt and expected, with the advent of democracy, that we would strengthen Yugoslavia in the economic sense and in the democratic sense. Unfortunately, something else happened, something quite different, and that was that the desires of certain - how shall I put this? - the desire of some people to step down from Yugoslavia, I'm sure they know why, the people who wanted secession, and also there was the desire of a certain section of the population to remain within Yugoslavia. And I quite honestly say I belong to that section of the population. I wanted to stay in the community we lived in because this community by its very nature is stronger than separation and disunity and fragmentation, in fact. So of course, one could feel a certain amount of fear on all sides; those who wanted to step down and secede, as well as those who wished to remain within Yugoslavia. The psyche of the people began to change as well quite suddenly. And until yesterday, we worked together, we drank coffee together, we took our meals together. We would go to market together, we would have picnics together. We would engage in cultural events, sports events. But quite suddenly there was this about-turn, a change of face. We were no longer motivated. We didn't have any desires for things of this kind. That's how it started. Then there was insecurity, people began to think about leaving the areas they lived in, especially those people and those ethnic groups who were the minority in certain regions. So the Serbs left the territories where the Muslims were the majority, or the Croats, and vice versa. And that's how it was. So there was a lack of security, there was uncertainty, there were a lot of contradictions. And I myself am unable to explain how this happened. When we were offered democracy in our own house, when we had the chance of living together, suddenly a disease seemed to eat away at us, and we seemed to be afraid of something or somebody was controlling us and moving us towards a different kind of life, a different way of life. So this is the sort of uncertainty that I myself felt. And to be quite frank, I found it very difficult to contend with. Perhaps it's a little strange, but this was even worse for me to be able to contend with than the war. Let me explain why: During the war, I didn't have much time to think, like many others. First of all, you had to fight for your own personal integrity. You had to see to the safety and security of your nearest and dearest, and do what you could, anything that was possible in those difficult times. Now, as to the period you're asking me about, there was enough leeway and room to think, to give thought to all these matters. And so I find it very difficult to think about those times, precisely because of the psychology that reigned at the time. And we physicians tend to call it a mass psychosis, if you like, if I can put it that way, this fear, these phobias as to what was going to happen and what was in store for people in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that very detailed and extensive answer, Doctor. Let's now move on to another period, the period after the 30th of April, and we're going to think about the period between the 30th of April and the 30th of September. We're going to focus on that period of time because that is the period we're interested in, the material time that we're focussing on. Where were you after the 30th of April, and what were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I was an active captain first class in the medical corps. That was my rank at the time. I was a doctor. And when the war started, I was in the medical health centre in Banja Luka. I worked as a doctor. I carried out my regular duties. I was in charge of examining the active-duty servicemen, their families, and pensioners, the retired officers, those who were covered by the military health fund. And as the war went on, I was transferred to the war unit, the so-called medical battalion. The medical battalion is -- was, during that war, was one of the largest medical mobile units, and I was the chief of the general first medical aid in that medical battalion, and I was in charge of treating those who were not seriously wounded. I was also in charge of organising the transport of the wounding, the so-called triage or the assessment of the wounded, and I would decide who were those who needed either surgical help or psychiatric help or decontamination and similar things. And I was also in charge of deciding who was to be transported into the nearest military medical centres. Throughout the entire war, the medical battalion was stationed in Banja Luka, in the military facilities there belonging to the barracks. The name of the barracks at the time was Dr. Mladen Stojanovic. This is where the wounded and the sick were taken. And in that garrison clinic, which had a department for internal diseases, a surgical department, a neuropsychiatric department, a department for those who were seriously wounded and for those who were slightly wounded, and this is what mostly took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the region covered by your unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Within the command of the 1st Corps, there was this medical battalion, and it covered the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. To put it that way, in the military terms, in professional terms of the military. So this is the area or the territory in the town of Banja Luka and the surrounding area of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that mostly Bosanska Krajina, by and large? Was that region Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, it also embraced Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to Banja Luka, did you also work during the war on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. We had mobile surgical teams belonging to the medical battalion. This was necessary. And during the war, it proved very useful. We had two surgical teams that were sent to various theatres of war, but not close to the front lines. They would keep in the rear, some 18 to 20 kilometres away from the front lines, and this is where they surgically treated the wounded and the sick. That was in Novi Grad, Doboj, Teslic, Glamoc, Mrkonjic. Wherever there was a need, wherever there were sick and wounded, we would send our surgical teams forward. And I was one of the organisers of their work, meaning I was the one who was in charge of sending those teams, for giving them all the necessary medical supplies and medicines to take with them, and the rest that was necessary for their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us the situation in Novi Grad, for example, when you were a member of that forward team in Novi Grad. What did it look like? Where did you work? Who were the ones who you treated? Can you provide us with a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: We worked in the surgery of the Novi Grad health centre. That is, in the facilities that were intended for health care. We had an x-ray machine there, a laboratory; we had all the technical facilities necessary to carry out such interventions. And in addition to that, we also could keep the patients so to say hospitalised after they had been surgically treated. And we treated all the wounded and all the sick from that area, from that theatre of war, belonging to the units who were deployed in the area. But also, this team and these people treated the civilian population in the area. I remember very well that there were not only Serbian population, but also Muslim and Croat population who were treated and extended medical, surgical, and any other aid that was necessary. If my memory serves me well, we have not turned anybody down because of their ethnicity, because they were of a different ethnicity. Doctors -- and as far as I can remember, that did not exist. It never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, you already belonged to the army of Republika Srpska. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. In May 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And us officers who originate from that part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given an opportunity to either return to Yugoslavia with the Yugoslav People's Army or to remain where we were at the time, in the then army of Republika Srpska. I opted for the latter because this is the area that I belonged to. My family lived in Banja Luka at the time. We had an apartment there. And one of the reasons for which I joined the army was the apartment that I was allocated by the army. And I started working on the 18th of April, and I got the apartment already in May. So that problem was solved. My parents were there. So at the moment, there was nothing that would tell me that I should withdraw with the army. I stayed there. I stayed put where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday evening, you did a sketch for me, a rough sketch of the military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would kindly ask the usher to put the document in front of you. The document is in B/C/S only. The document is not in English. We were afraid that maybe we wouldn't use the proper terms and we left it to the interpreters to translate this scheme correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This document would be D50. Any objections? I can't see any. So therefore, admitted into evidence, D50.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got a translation, so I don't know what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but as we did in the past, whatever the probative value may be at the end of the day, it's for a better understanding of the testimony of the witness before us today, it should be admitted into evidence, D50B. And the translation can be found on the transcript of today, page 12 following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we'll compose the translated version after today's day, so we'll use this transcript and compose the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But if it could be explained and read out at the same time by the witness, we have it already on the transcript, and it saves work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Pusac, can you please -- I don't know whether you can see the document on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the screen, you cannot point. You will have to take the pointer on your right-hand side and point on the ELMO, on the paper. So point to the things that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please go through this table and explain to us nonmilitary persons what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you immediately, I am a member of the medical corps, and I am a medical colonel. I did not complete any military academies, so I was a civilian when I joined the army. I graduated from the civilian medical university and that's how I joined the army. So I do not have such a broad knowledge in order to be able to present things to you in military terms. But this is as much as I should understand, and in that sense, I would like to inform you. So this is a chain of command that I'm familiar with, and that is shown clearly in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what are you pointing to? You're pointing to the top box.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, the Supreme Command, the Supreme Commander is the president of state at the time, the president of the Republika Srpska, who issues orders to the main staff, that is, the commander of the main staff. He then issues orders to corps, to lower units in the corps command and units and institutions who are directly reporting to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are two parallel squares.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. Orders are given to the subordinate units, to the units and institutions of the main staff. At the same time, the main staff can issue orders to the corps commands. Corps commands issue orders to the units on the strength of the respective corps. Those were brigades and independent battalions. This command issues orders to the units on the strength of the respective brigades and independent battalions. And those units are battalions and companies. So the command in this square issues orders down the chain to battalions and companies which are subordinate units, and then to platoons, squads, and finally, the orders reach troops as the basic units in the army. So this is the vertical chain of issuing orders that was in place during the war, and this is something that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the medical part of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the medical battalion. And the medical battalion was on the strength of the 1st Corps. However, the commander of the medical battalion received orders from the assistant commander for the rear or logistics of the 1st Corps. So the medical corps is a service in the army, and it is not a branch of the army. So the medical corps is not a military operational unit. It doesn't carry out any other tasks. The only tasks it carries out belong to the area of providing medical care, providing health care. And we received our orders not directly. It could happen that orders were given by the corps commander, but mostly it was -- our orders from received from the assistant commander for the logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That person, in any case, was a military person, an officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The assistant commander of the 1st Corps for logistics was an officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of your superior at the time? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Dr. Slobodan Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an active serviceman? Was he an officer? Did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an active serviceman, an officer, with the rank of medical colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the military units, were they divided according to the municipalities, or did they cover several municipalities? Can you tell us that? Do you know about that? So we're not talking about the medical corps itself, but generally.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The medical corps was composed on the basis of several municipalities, and I do know that other units were composed of three -- members from three or more municipalities. As far as I know, there were no units from just one place bearing one name and being active for one territory. They were always composed of servicemen from three or more municipalities. Usually, the municipalities that were closest, close by. Whereas the medical battalion, at the beginning of the war, in terms of cadres, had members not only from the nearby communities but from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina; from Sarajevo, from Mostar, and from Tuzla and so on. So at the beginning of the war, at the very start, the composition including servicemen not from one or several municipalities, but from a large number of municipalities, because we needed surgeons, we needed ophthalmologists, and so on, and that's where we found them; all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we're talking about the combat units, then they were usually composed and covered the territory of two or three municipalities; composed of people from there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, before we leave this document D50B, you were kind enough to describe the content of this document, but could you please also be kind enough just read out what we can see in the text of the boxes, for our better understanding from --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, perhaps we can do it this way: Could you place a number before each of the boxes, and then read them out. Place number 1, and then read out what it says in box number 1. You need not go into explanations, just read out what it says on the piece of paper. And please leave it on the overhead projector, so we can see.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Box number 1 says: "Supreme Command." Then it says: "Supreme Commander, the president of the state." Number 2: "Main staff of the army. The main staff commander." Number 3: "Corps commands." Number 4: "Units and institutions of the main staff." Number 5: "The commands of units from the corps, brigades, and independent battalions." Number 6: "The commands of units from the composition of the brigades and independent battalions, battalions and companies." Number 7: "Platoons." Number 8: "Squads." Number 9: "Troops or soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, would you please be so kind and allocate your own position within this table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In box number 5, it says, "Independent battalion." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that where you were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the medical battalion to which you belonged at that time? Was that the top level medical unit in Republika Srpska; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It was a military hospital, too. That's what it was called. It was the military hospital of the main staff. However, in that area, the Krajina area, the military medical institutions, apart from the medical centre which was not able to provide the services that the battalion could provide, there were no larger medical units, or rather, institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the corps command? Did the corps command command the medical battalion via the assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the first box which relates to the Supreme Command, and when we get into the real meat or structure of the army itself, could you tell us what the relationship is between the army and the civilian authorities? And I'm thinking about the civilian authorities at municipal level. Who issues orders to whom? How do you come into contact with them? Through which ministries? Could you explain that to us a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The army was completely autonomous and independent. As far as I know, all the units in the sense of control and command and the chain of command is concerned, and in my own area, which I can speak about, we would receive orders, all our orders, only from our direct superior, the corps command; that is to say, the assistant commander for logistics, especially in the Banja Luka Municipality, for example. There was never, at least as far as I know, a document or -- nor do I remember that we received orders from any civilian authority, or vice versa. We were not in a situation in which we could order them anything. I worked as a doctor myself, of course, so that organisation was within that sphere. And I'm sure you're interested in hearing about the strengths of the units and how we did that. That went through the Ministry of Defence. So as the medical battalion, we would send in a request to the Ministry of Defence for personnel, for cadres to be sent in to us. We would say we need doctors of such and such a profile; neuropsychiatrists, surgeons, for example, an orthopaedist, a vascular surgeon. We would say what we required and then the Ministry of Defence, having received our requests and having lists of conscripts and recruits, including doctors, would gather together the necessary people of these professional profiles and send them into the medical battalion. And that was the procedure throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to manpower, could you contact the Municipal Assembly directly yourself, the Municipal Assemblies of certain municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No, that was not the procedure we followed, either officially, in formal terms, or in practice. We could do nothing outside the procedure prescribed by law. So as I say, and to the best of my knowledge, that kind of thing was out of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that this was out of the question, as you say, and that you are aware of that, but we have to clarify certain points for trial purposes. So I would like to ask you whether you ever contacted the Crisis Staff of any municipality when you needed cadres.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, this term "Crisis Staff," and the institution itself, the concept itself, is not quite clear to me even to this day, the way in which it existed and functioned. And I say quite honestly and frankly that I do not remember -- and of course, this was absolutely prohibited by law, and I don't ever remember a case where anybody intentionally or unintentionally from the medical department of the army or the medical battalion would contact the Crisis Staff for anything or vice versa; they would not contact us, so I have no knowledge about that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to manpower and the professional people you needed, could you contact the health centre or hospital for the doctors you needed and medical staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The procedure was to contact the ministry and its departments. In practice, what would happen was that the ministry, without looking at the rationality and actual requirements of a particular medical institution, would send us the important professionals, doctors, from a medical institution. They would write a letter to that effect, to the medical department, to say that something should be done for one doctor to be replaced or sent back to the health institution where he had worked previously because he was needed there. His services were needed there. Of course, if a radiologist was irreplaceable and you had an x-ray in Banja Luka and now suddenly the Ministry of Defence decided to send the radiologist to the medical battalion, that meant that the health institution and the x-ray machine would be left without its professional, without the radiologist. So there would sometimes be two parallel requests to the medical battalion and the institution, but this was not obligatory procedure either by the medical battalion or the health institution in question. So they did sometimes, medical institutions would sometimes send in requests for us to return their physicians to them. But as I say, the official formal procedure always went through the department within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have just been talking about a case in which the health centre sends in a request to the army. How was this done? Could they order the army to send back the doctor who had been mobilised, or was this drafted in the form of a request?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know about other units. I don't know that anybody -- actually, these were tabled in the form of requests, drafted in the form of requests. And they prevailed upon us to exercise an understanding for their position. It was not an order because what would an army be if it could receive orders from different sources? Who would weigh up the orders, give greater weight to one order as opposed to another?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself worked in the medical and health department of the army, if I can put it that way. Could you tell us, please, before the war, did the army have a separate health system, medical system, apart from the civilian system, beginning with the fund for medical assistance and the institutions providing medical services themselves?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. Both before the war and during the war, and even up until quite recently in Republika Srpska, that was the situation. That is to say, there was a military fund for medical insurance, for medical insurees, so this medical fund ensured insurance for the active-duty army personnel, the members -- the family members of the active-duty servicemen, recruits, military pensioners, and members -- family members of military pensioners, retired military personnel, and the reservists, the reserve composition, the recruits when they were undergoing training, and during the war when they were engaged in combat. All injuries suffered, medical assistance was provided for by the medical departments of the army, and they were insured by the medical army insurance fund.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army have its military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take the following example: You were involved in a traffic accident as a military man. Did the civilian police force -- were the civilian policemen able to carry out their job without the presence of a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No. Any incidents involving a military vehicle or an army member, active-duty soldier or officer and the entire staff of the army, in fact, all the members of an army, all the civilian police could do was to come out on site. But the military police had to come on site to carry out their scene of crime investigation. We had military courts. And after the investigation had been conducted, the whole proceedings would have been referred to the military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in addition to the independent provision of health care to the military personnel, there was also the independent judiciary which carried out procedures against the military servicemen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This included the military police, the military prosecutor's office, and the military courts at various levels, various instance courts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you something about the period prior to April 1992. When you lived in Banja Luka, did you notice the arrival of refugees from Slovenia, Croatia during the years 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course. Every citizen of Banja Luka could see that. Very often, those were columns of people carrying all sorts of things. It was an image across the world, and I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, did you, in the army, start feeling the lack of the necessary medicines - antibiotics and similar things - and how did the situation develop up to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course we did. Although we had some stock at our disposal, the stock dwindled and we were seized by panic because there is nothing worse than when you, as you a doctor, see a wounded or sick person, he is looking at you, and you have nothing to give him, you don't have everything that is necessary for you to provide him with the adequate help. We managed as we could. We cooperated with the International National Committee of the Red Cross, with Medecins Sans Frontieres, and personally, I maintained contact as the person in charge of medical supplies, and especially the dressings, injections, syringes, and we really could feel that, and we hoped that this unfortunate war would be over quickly, in a month or two months. And as we were preparing for the war and thinking about maybe amassing bigger stocks, none of us really made a good assessment about the duration and the scope of the war. We never foresaw the wounds that we were going to see. We were taken by surprise, and we did as we could on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you did what you could, you did what you could, you mean you maintained the supplies to the extent you could. Did the army have its logistics? What were the logistical services that you had?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: We had a so-called basis for supplies, and we had medical supplies. And when it comes to the medical supplies and medicines and drugs, this base was our logistics, and it made an integral part of the army. And as far as the existence of other logistical services is concerned, we had the quartermaster supplies, the medical supply services. And when I say quartermaster supplies, that implies the clothing, the food. We also had technical service. We had our financial service, our construction service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of these services integral parts of the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these active units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course. They were either units or institutions, but they were military institutions or units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in addition to combat units and logistics units or services, were there, to the best of your knowledge, after April of 1992, any paramilitary units in the territory of Krajina? How much would you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It is possible that there were paramilitary units. I don't know the names and their size, the area where they were active, because this was not something that I had to find out. But in any case, they were not under the military command. I only know from conversations that wherever their activities could be prevented, if they did something of nonmilitary nature, that the army would intercept them and that the army would prevent that. But I really am not familiar with that, I wouldn't be able to tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking about the manpower and the replenishment of military units. And for that, as a military unit, you would turn to the Ministry of Defence whenever you needed technical equipment. But that was more the case of the construction service, when they needed machinery.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As regards medical equipment and things that are necessary for the medical corps, we would go to our superior command. And when it came to the supplies of materiel and supplies, we would go to the command, not to the Ministry of Defence or its departments. We would contact the Ministry of Defence and its departments only when we needed personnel, when we need people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the right to, for example, commandeer part of the hospital if you wanted to carry out your procedures there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No, my unit couldn't do that. It did not have legal authority to mobilise or commandeer parts of a space or somebody's offices. It was the superior command who could do that. For example, we received an order from our superior command, from the assistant commander for logistics, to set up a surgical outpatients clinic in Novi Grad, in the health centre of Novi Grad. That is when we would go to that institution, to the health centre there, and we would meet with people who had already worked there. We would show them that order, and we would agree on the use of the area, but certainly not at the expense of their work, because there had already been their services there, so we would reach an agreement on working together. For example, in Novi Grad, at the time, they didn't have a surgeon, so we agreed that in addition in providing for our wounded, we would also provide surgical care for the civilian population. Not only Novi Grad, but throughout the war, everywhere wherever we went, we relied on the civilian institutions to complete the work that we started. So they would be the ones who would take over from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, during the war, or after the war, was it possible that the president of a municipality would issue orders to you, or maybe the president of the Executive Board or the president of the Crisis Staff of a municipality? So was there such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Let me just tell you one thing: For example, the Ministry of Health and the Minister of Health were not satisfied with the regulations which prevented them from issuing orders or sending requests to us for something to be carried out. To tell you the truth, they were not very happy with that situation. Sometimes they were angry, even jealous, and the way they saw it is that the Ministry of Health should be in the position to issue orders to a smaller medical unit. For example, if that unit took their epidemiologist, they thought that they should be able to have that epidemiologist returned to them immediately. But they couldn't do it, they couldn't do it before the war or throughout the war. Now things are changing. Reforms are on the way of the medical services, of the judiciary in Republika Srpska, so things are changing because reforms are on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These changes were initiated after the signing of the Dayton accords? Can you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your unit, were there people of non-Serbian ethnicity during the war? And what was the composition of the families of active-duty servicemen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In the introduction, I told you that we were so mixed, and at the same time, there was a strong integrity in among the people. And that could be witnessed in the military structures. Almost every second military family was a family with -- of a mixed marriage. So Serbs, Muslims, they were all intermixed. And in the beginning, in the medical battalion, there were Muslims, Croats, active officers. And during the war, there were even those who stayed on. I can give you -- I can tell you that at the beginning of the war, for example, there was Teofik Kovacevic, I believe he was a major. There was Miroslav Bakovic. They were active officers who were professionals and who were experts in the organisation of medical service. They were experts on the deployment of medical units. There was Mehmed, a Bosniak, a radiologist who lived in Banja Luka throughout the war, and he is still there, living in Banja Luka. There was also a friend of mine, Dr. Alija Kustric, an excellent expert who was there up until almost the end of the war, and he worked in the medical battalion. In my building, there was a lady doctor, Amela Ceric, who lived there throughout the war and still lives there. And she belongs to the well-known Ceric family. And those are the people that come to mind first. So the battalion was not a Serbian battalion during the war. In amongst us doctors, there were always people of various ethnicities. There were also nurses of different ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your colleagues abandon the ranks of the JNA after the beginning of war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course. People were leaving. Some people were demobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the examples of your colleagues, once they left the JNA, joining the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I remember a specialist in internal medicine, Dr. Redzepagic from Sarajevo, who was a member of the medical corps in 1991. He left us, together with the majority of doctors from Sarajevo of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they driven away or did they leave of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: They simply failed to show up for work. And this is what I was talking about, the fear that people felt. And I can really not hold it against the people for being afraid. Everybody wanted to stay closer to their families during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those war months, the spring and summer of 1992, in fact, did you happen to hear of the existence of a body which was called the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I did, but I never actually thought about what the Crisis Staff actually was, who made it up, and so on. Because us officers, we were not able to be a member of any political party or delve in politics at all, any Executive Board or anything like that. And the Crisis Staff was something that was not a military association, and in that sense, and also because of my duties as a doctor, I must say that I don't know enough about this body. I haven't got very much information about it nor do I know whether -- that we cooperated or received any instructions from them. Had we done so, I probably would have known more about it and could tell you more about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him? How did you come to meet him? Could you tell us a little bit about that, please, and about him.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, I first met my colleague from my native town. They were two villages, actually two neighbouring villages that we both come from, and I knew -- we knew each other as children. We're not too far apart in years either. But perhaps my first recollections of him are when he started working in Omarska, which is where I worked, too. And that was sometime in the 1990s. Before that, I had heard my parents talking about him. They said that another young man, a doctor -- had become a doctor, graduated from the faculty of medicine and was working in Omarska, too. And my father told me that he had been to see the doctor in question and that he was pleasantly surprised. He said that he was my father and he conveyed greetings from Dr. Pusac. And so when he met the doctor, he felt that he was first and foremost a good man, a good professional. And having heard all this from my father, I wanted to meet him and to talk to him and to hear what was wrong with my father, what he thought after having examined him. So my contacts with the man - and I'm very happy to see him now once again - were natural, quite natural. I was very pleased to see that there were several of us from my own native region. He exuded a very humane quality. He exuded a breadth of knowledge and understanding which I myself would like to have, and it is only someone with human qualities of this kind who can be a good doctor, too. He said he had professional ambitions, he wanted to go forward in the medical field. At the time, I wasn't able -- I couldn't have said that he would have actually engaged in politics later on, but you know, we doctors do have this breadth of outlook. And when I think back -- of course, I didn't think about it at the time, I didn't give it much thought, but that is possible, too. Because as I say, the democracy, the advent of democracy offered us intellectuals different opportunities. We had rid ourselves of the communist yoke, and we were able to fight for what we wanted for our profession, for our professional training, for organising the health service, to get closer to Europe. Because I don't think that, in the name of us doctors, on our behalf, anybody could represent us better than somebody from our own profession. We are better represented by doctors than we would be by, say, civil engineers. So that was probably the reason why Dr. -- why my colleague Mr. Milomir Stakic engaged in that type of activity, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you later on members of one particular body which was linked to your work, the main board of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the main board of the Red Cross in the regional section, Red Cross section. First of all, I was a member of the presidency of the society of physicians. We had a society of physicians of Republika Srpska, first of all. And my colleague, Dr. Stakic, was a member of the presidency, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know him better then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I got to know him even better during that period of time, because he had engaged in certain activities in the municipality within his profession. And this had an impact on me. I saw that somebody who had all his professional duties to carry out, nevertheless had the desire and succeeded in helping us activate this society, our society of physicians, and to give it a name as an institution, so that it could be of assistance to our colleagues, doctors in the different medical institutions. So this was a professional association of physicians. We didn't talk about politics or any -- engage in any party politics. We discussed our own professional medical problems. And in that sense, the profile and structure of a man of his calibre made an impact on me. I saw it to be positive and something that was very necessary in our midst. And we said that it would be a very good thing if he could come as often as possible so that we could cooperate. I am the secretary-general even today of the society of physicians of Republika Srpska, and as an institution, we have a health or medical chamber, as we call it, and we have engaged in the reform of the medical service which has taken great strides forward and has grown closer to Europe. And my colleague, Dr. Stakic, took the part in that work of that particular body.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The estimate of time you would need in addition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Half an hour, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you for this. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And let us continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Pusac, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back a little. You were saying that you were pleased to see Dr. Stakic today. I'm sure you don't mean you're pleased to see him in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Together with Dr. Stakic, you were a member of the society of physicians of Republika Srpska, as you said. And you said that you got to know him better working in that society.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I got to know more about my colleague, and I was able to confirm the opinion I had of him when I met him for the first time. And that is that he was a peaceful, quiet man with a breadth of vision. He emanates humane qualities. And at the time, I saw that I had before me a highly professional person who would go forward in his profession, who would help people professionally and organisationally, promote the level of health care and protection, and the health service in general. Medical science as well. And that his presence, quite simply, was a pleasure to see. It was nice to have him around. He would always make proposals at meetings which were realistic. They were good proposals, well thought out. And I saw that even in the conditions that prevailed in our own country and in those wartime conditions, medical care could be promoted so that we could help people and do what we had been professionally trained to do. And that's the impression that stayed with me. It was a very strong impression. He made a strong impression on me, and I can rightly say, I think, that I don't think that man could even think of doing something, let alone actually doing it, something which was outside, not only a doctor's dignity, but human dignity as well. Outside the realms of those dictates, and particularly not to one's own people. And when I say "one's own people," I mean all the people that lived in the area we lived and worked in, and as I say, there were Muslims and Croats and Serbs all living there together. Because Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially the Krajina region, was Yugoslavia in miniature. There were strong bonds linking us together. That's how we were brought up. Our roots were there in that territory. We were patriotically brought up, and I don't know of anybody in that environment, in Omarska and in the region, who had any other views at that time and did anything other than humane acts to help one's fellow man, which is nice to experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In talking to Dr. Stakic, did you ever happen to notice that he had any prejudices of any kind? Did you ever note any prejudices towards Muslims, Croats, or other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No. Never. It never entered my head, let alone see anything that have kind or hear from others that he had done anything of that kind. Even today, I ask people I encounter what their opinion is of Dr. Stakic, and they confirm my own views of him, the locals, the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic express any kind of hatred or hostility towards the Muslims, Croats, and other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From talking to Dr. Stakic, did you ever hear him express any discriminatory views, vis-a-vis the Muslims, Croats, and other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, from talking to Dr. Stakic, were you able to conclude, or rather, did you manage to gauge what Dr. Stakic thought about Croats, Muslims, and other non-Serbs? Did you gain an impression of his views about them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, I can't define and assess something along the lines of what he thought, especially not in any negative sense, no negative connotations. I never heard any words or saw any pictures or read anything that he might have said about those ethnic groups in prejudicial terms, underestimating or undervaluing them in any way. Even in the health centre of Omarska, for example, Dr. Ibro Beglerbegovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dr. Ibrobegovic"] was a Muslim, the doctor was a Muslim, and I can say that he felt more Serb than the Serbs in the town of Omarska because he had been accepted by all of us, by one and all. And he accepted by us. And I know that this particular doctor, a Muslim doctor, cooperated very well with Dr. Stakic and had a very positive view of Dr. Stakic. So I have nothing which would prompt me in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About this doctor, the Bosniak doctor, the name has been entered into the transcript wrongly. Would you state the name of the doctor again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name. Could the doctor repeat the doctor's name, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Dr. Ibrahim Beglerbegovic. And the nickname we referred to him by was "Ibro."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of Dr. Stakic's arrest? Did you hear when he was arrested and transferred to The Hague? And could you tell us what you thought and felt at the time. Could you tell us a bit about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I just couldn't believe it. I could never have imagined that this kind of man with the kind of human characteristics that I have described here as a colleague, a friend, a local man living in the same environment, could have done anything to warrant being arrested. So that it was a shock. It was a great shock. And when I learned of it, my first reaction was one of disbelief. But when I learned that it was true, then I thought, well, he's going before an Honourable Trial Chamber, an Honourable Tribunal, perhaps they need him to provide information because he knows more about the events that went on in Prijedor. And I thought that his stay here, the time he spent here and that justice would prevail, and I still can't come to terms with the idea that the man could have done any bad things, thought any bad thoughts or ordered anything bad of the kind of allegations that have been made and charges brought against him. So it is my opinion -- or rather, I have no arguments, no information, no facts or knowledge of him doing anything other than the kind of work that I have described him as doing, being the man he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about the population being ethnically mixed, and especially the military personnel and their families. Did Serb officers, members of the former JNA, and later on, the army of Republika Srpska often marry members of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Of course. This was something that couldn't be avoided. Before the war, it was absolutely normal and one didn't choose whom to fall in love with. One could choose, but one didn't really pay attention. One didn't think too much about what the person's -- the other person's name was. The only concern was whether somebody was in love or not. And I believe that this is still the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the percentages of mixed marriages in the social structure of the former Yugoslavia was the highest amongst the officers of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I believe that this was the case, because this is a structure which served and professionally worked all over the territory, across Yugoslavia, from Slovenia to Macedonia. Its officers had an opportunity to marry women of other ethnic groups. A Serbian would go to Bosnia, would marry a Muslim girl, a Slovenian would go to Serbia and marry a Serbian girl. And that was normal. It was the way people worked and the way people lived. It was only natural that things like that should happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So officers would often be sent from one place to another to serve in the army, and that occurred throughout their service in the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your mind, can one expect from the command personnel of an army that is so ethnically mixed to plan a persecution of people on ethnic and religious backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: This is not naturally possible, because it is like in one family, as if one family were to design a plan according to which ones would destroy the others, and nobody would know about the other plan. How would it be possible for a large family such was Bosnia and Herzegovina that a plan was designed without the wives, the children knowing about that plan, that people of different ethnic groups living in the same family wouldn't know about that plan? Such a thing could not exist in terms of any such plan being designed. And what I claim is that this is something impossible, and it was something that was absolutely unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, please, to refrain from those hypothetical questions and more general questions. The answer given by the witness maybe will be related to the period of time and the area of former Yugoslavia, but of course, this can't be answered in general because, unfortunately, history has shown during the last centuries that even when he had ethnically mixed societies, this was, unfortunately, never an obstacle for starting war and armed conflicts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were also talking about paramilitary formations. Do you know anything about the killing of Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I heard about that in 1992. Banja Luka is a bit away from Prijedor. I heard that that had happened, but the details of that event, I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the reaction of his unit was when their commander was killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I heard that some people thought that this killing could have been avoided, that they were unhappy with the military unit that they belonged to, and that's when they decided to leave that unit. They disobeyed the military orders. Whether they became members of a paramilitary unit or not, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher now to show the witness the document we submitted today, number 00861611. It's in B/C/S. And the English version is 00938569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally marked as D51.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pusac, we did not have a chance to look at this document, so I'm not going to ask you about its contents. Maybe the Honourable Chamber or the OTP will want to know something about the contents. But what I'm interested in is the heading of this document. We see here that it says, "Military secret, strictly confidential." Below that: "Coded. To be delivered immediately." Can you please tell us who is the sender of this report? When, and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It was the command of the 1st Krajina Corps that sent this report on the 13th of June, 1992, at 1700 hours. And it was sent to the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, it was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Regular combat report."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it happen that such a document, such a report, a regular combat report marked as a military secret, strictly confidential, so could it happen that such a document was sent to a civilian body?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No. According to the chain of command, this could only be sent to the superior command, but also to a subordinate command, according to the hierarchy or the vertical line that I explained at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need this document any more. We are finished with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D51A and B respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like to have the usher now to show the witness another document which we also received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document was reporting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please wait until we have the document. Thank you. Provisionally marked D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was received by the Defence from the OTP, and the English version is numbered 03005262. And the B/C/S version is 00820936. Doctor, again, we have not had an opportunity to look at this document carefully, but would you please tell us what this document is about. What can you read in the heading? Who is the author of this document? Who put it together? And what is ordered by this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: This is an order by the commander of the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska, again strictly confidential. And the date is the 3rd of July, 1992. Its title is: "Changes in the organisation and establishment of the army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is ordered by this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It is ordered to the army of Republika Srpska to carry out the following organisation and establishment changes. And then (a), form in the 1st Krajina Corps, so the order refers to the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible for such a document or any document of similar sort to be delivered to the civilian bodies of authority in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please find page 11 in this document. And can you please read the first paragraph. In the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Page 4, at the beginning. The beginning of the page. Sorry, it's the third page, bottom of the page, under (c): "Changes of the mobilisation" - under 1 - "in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then to be continued on the next page. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read on page 11, under (c).

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Changes to the basic mobilisation plan." Under 1: "In the 1st Krajina Corps, (a) the 5th Kozara Light Infantry Brigade is assigned Prijedor as peacetime location and mobilisation point instead of Banja Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10914 to 10917. Luka. Other elements of the basic mobilisation plan remain the same."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible that when a location of a military unit was assigned, that civilian bodies of authority took part in that, or was it exclusively in the military purview?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It was in the purview of the relevant department of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any longer for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Didn't we want also to read out (d)?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I just wanted to emphasise Prijedor region, but if Your Honours want, we can proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The only question is when I read Kozara there, is it also related to Prijedor, or it may be a name of a similar town or hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can ask Dr. Pusac. Maybe he knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, could you read out the next paragraph under (d), please, because the Kozara link was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Changes to establishment in the 1st communications Battalion of the 1st Krajina Corps. At the following station, re: Communication nodes to the battalion established in Kozara consisting of four noncommissioned officers and 13 soldiers; Svinjar, consisting of four noncommissioned officers and 13 soldiers; Vlasic consisting of four noncommissioned officers and 13 soldiers." This is perhaps linked to the communication point. Quite possibly it was Kozara, but this isn't my profession, so actually I can't explain that any further to you. What we can see here is that we are talking about the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Krajina Corps to which you belonged. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. There might have been a Kozara node or communications point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when we read "Vlasic," is it related to such a communication point at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly, but I can't say for sure because that is not the area of my own expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D52A and B correspondingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're on the subject of Mount Vlasic, I don't know how far you yourself know, but do you happen to know that it was on this mountain that fighting took place throughout the war, and that parts of the mountain would come under the control of one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the proffer to this Honourable Trial Chamber, I stated that in the Krajina region, you yourself were there until June 1992. However, as we received your medical documents only yesterday, and looking at those documents, could you tell us until when you were in the Krajina region and the time you spent undergoing medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to call upon the usher to show the medical documents to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, first of all, when you were talking to me, you thought that you had actually left the region at the end of June. But looking through your medical documents, you saw that you were actually there for the whole of the month of July. So would you show us the document that we can refer to when talking about the actual time you left the region in 1992. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the end of July. I didn't remember the month correctly, because it was 1992. So ten or 11 years ago, but I do know that I was ill. And then I didn't quite remember, when you asked me about the events in Prijedor, when this actually took place. I wasn't able to link up what I knew about the events going on and where I was at the time. But of course, I did remember that I was ill, but I failed to remember the exact date. So at the end of July, after the 20th of July, I felt some changes. I had trouble with my hearing and system of balance, my equilibrium, and I went to the military medical centre, the outpatients department there, and the ear, eye, and throat doctor took a look at me. But my state deteriorated. And on the 14th of August, the ambulance took me to the medical military academy. This was an emergency, and I had to stay there for one month, undergoing treatment. I was on sick leave several months after that outside my unit, probably up to the month of October. So I wasn't an active-duty physician at the time I was on sick leave because I had these health problems. And that is why I did not remember -- I couldn't have any recollection of what was going on during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the document on the overhead projector? That's the document you're referring to. Is that correct? Dr. Pusac, is that the document? Can you see the document on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're shaking your head, and that can't be recorded in the transcript, so could you give us an audible answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read it out to us, please, so that Their Honours know what it's about. You can read from the document or from the screen, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, it is a discharge sheet from the clinic for ear, nose, and throat, of the medical military academy in Belgrade, Pusac Momir. I was captain first class at that time from Banja Luka. The date I was admitted is the 14th of August, 1992. And the diagnosis was hypacusis acuta of the auris dexter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the diagnosis in Latin, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But in Serbian, in simple layman's language, it means that the circulation in one artery had been disturbed. The artery that is used for hearing. So it enables us to hear. And the circulation in that artery had stopped, had been interrupted, which meant that I was hard of hearing. And this led to an upset in my body's equilibrium. It is a very serious condition and very unpleasant for the person suffering from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour, we would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the submissions by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Chamber has briefly discussed this. And I think what is relevant for our case is the mere fact that you were only -- that you would have been in hospital during this period of time you mentioned, and you gave us the other data. But it seems to be necessary today to protect the personal data, especially health data, and when admitting such a document into evidence, there's always the risk that such a document on your personal data will fall into wrong hands. And therefore, the Trial Chamber does not admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we just wanted to show, when this gentleman is cross-examined, so that everybody knows that he wasn't in the area in this period of time. And we agree that it's not crucial as evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
