utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a military man, of course, a doctor by profession, did you know or were you aware of the existence of any paramilitary formations, paramilitary units, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you know of the existence of the Patriotic League, the Croatian Defence Council, two cases in point?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear of their existence. But this -- I was never in a position to learn any more about them or have any contacts with them, with formations of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear -- have you heard of the fighting and the entry of regular forces of the Republic of Croatia into Bosanski Brod at the beginning of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that. And that's round about the time that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started, in fact. It was sometime in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear about the slaughter in Sijekovac also in March?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I would have to have heard because the information media publicised it. It was in all the papers and in the media, so quite logically, I knew about it, I was able to come by that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pusac. That concludes my examination-in-chief. You will now be asked questions by my learned colleague of the Prosecution. And after that, Their Honours will have the opportunity of asking you their own questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution wishes to make an application to defer the cross-examination of this witness. I discussed this with the Defence in the break and said that I was going to make the application and suggested that they call the next witness in chief and we'll cross-examine both witnesses tomorrow, but that's not possible for the next witness. The reason I'm asking is because there are a number of issues that the witness testified about today which weren't in the original proffer and we only received the amended proffer yesterday. And it also has caused a problem because of the Brdjanin case and the Stakic case being heard at the same time. And Ms. Korner raised the issue and asked that we only sit in the mornings this week because of the problem. So what I'm suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can cut the story short. The next witness will be available as of 1.30. That's the brand-new information I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's impossible, Your Honour. The Defence is not prepared to proceed with the witness because, in anticipation of what we learned yesterday, we expected this witness to go on most if not the entire day today, so we did not meet with our witness to prepare our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt. At the end of the day yesterday - you can read it from the transcript - we asked the parties to be prepared to start with the second witness as of today. So let's see how we can proceed. It may be a possibility for the next minutes to proceed with questions by the Judges and then defer the cross-examination, say, either by the end of tomorrow or on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just explain, Your Honour, or at least make an offer of proof for our position. We, in scheduling the witnesses, would have prepared the witness last night, instead prepared this witness at the request of the OTP. Naturally, both witnesses are here. They are generally ready to proceed. If the Witness number 72 is going to testify today, I would have spent time preparing her last night. Given the situation that we have two witnesses remaining and three days left, counting today, again, with all due respect to the Court, we are moving the case along. The urgency -- although the OTP has requested, and we don't have an objection to them getting a little more time, our witness will be prepared to proceed tomorrow morning at 9.00. That's our scheduling. I know representations were made last night. Generally, they are prepared. We would like, however, to do our job as efficiently and professionally as we can. So we would ask the Court, respectfully, to proceed with that witness tomorrow morning. We can conclude, I think, both witnesses no later than Friday afternoon, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I please add something? The reason why we're not prepared is because of the change in the order of witnesses. Witness number 58 was supposed to be testifying today, which was a very lengthy witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So taking into account the submissions by the parties yesterday, taking into account that it was well-known and established already yesterday that Witness number 58 would not be available today, taking into account that it was on the request by the Prosecution to hear this witness today and not tomorrow, we have to proceed as planned. And we have to regard the Prosecution as one unit. And therefore, it is necessary and it's mandatory to proceed. Maybe, if need may be, the Trial Chamber would be prepared to start with their line of questions, if the Defence so agrees, before the cross-examination. But the cross-examination has to take place today. And then we start with the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution agrees that the cross-examination can start today. But in the Rule 65 ter conference last Thursday, Your Honours did say that if we received an amended proffer late, then we could have additional time to prepare for cross-examination. And as Your Honours have heard this morning, a number of issues were raised by this witness which were new to us. We received the amended proffer yesterday. So we would just ask for some time to prepare the documents that we want to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will take the opportunity to compare this morning's transcript with the proffer, because to be honest, personally, I did not see these major discrepancies between the proffer we received in due time opposed to that what we heard from you, Dr. Pusac, today. Therefore, it's hereby decided the cross-examination will take place this afternoon. And if on request of the Prosecution, the Judges should start with their line of questions, we are prepared to do so. The trial stays adjourned until 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.58 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the Prosecution, what is now your choice? Let the Judges start, or do you want to start?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honours; I'm happy to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the floor is yours. If you could please close the door. Cross-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, could you just move the -- so I have a line of sight. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pusac, you mentioned in your evidence earlier this morning Zoran Karlica. Do you believe that he's a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No -- or rather, I don't know. I was just responding to the question. When asked whether I had heard about the killing of Karlica, I said I had heard about it, but I really don't know who he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware that he was active in operations in Western Slavonia in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or that Zoran Karlica's unit was part of the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I assume he was in the 43rd, but I don't have that piece of information. It wasn't my area of expertise. I wasn't interested in things like that, so I can't say for sure whether he was a member of the unit or was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Veljko Milenkovic, who was the commander of the paramilitary group the Wolves of Bihac [phoen], are you aware that he fought with units of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I heard that he was a fighter and that he had taken part in the war, but what formation or unit he belonged to himself, I really can't say. I don't know. If you ask me about the medical corps, perhaps I could give you an answer. But I really don't know the answer to questions like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your evidence earlier that paramilitaries were not under the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please quote the page of the transcript, that we have it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour. It's page 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still stand by this assertion, that paramilitaries were not under military command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't have any official information about that. I personally don't know, am not aware that they were. I really can't say. I don't know. As far as I know, in the military command, you had the active-military units. They came under the military command. And with respect to the medical corps, I don't know that there was a paramilitary medical corps or that it was under our command, higher up the chain of command or down the line. So once again, it's not my area. I really can't answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly my point. And just so that we're clear, you don't know whether paramilitary units came under the military command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated -- for Their Honours' and the Defence's benefit, page 11 of the transcript this morning -- that in May 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army, i.e., the JNA, withdrew from the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true that officers who originated from Bosnia-Herzegovina went back there, but it's not true that the JNA withdrew from the entire territory. In fact, the units that existed in the 5th Corps were simply renamed within the 1st Krajina Corps. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As far as I know from those times, the active units of the Yugoslav People's Army, with all the equipment and military materiel, and all the medical equipment, withdrew. Now, to what extent and how many units remained, what percentage stayed on and what percentage withdrew, I really don't know. I can't give you facts and figures about that. But I do know officially that I personally had the possibility of going back to Yugoslavia and to continue my duties there working in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's true that the JNA didn't withdraw the equipment, but it was kept there, and in fact it was simply a transformation and not a withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, part of the equipment was withdrawn. And I'm sure that another portion remained where it was, the equipment that belonged to that territory originally and which had taken part and was used in security during peacetime, to provide security for the facilities that were jointly built. So the fact is that that kind of military materiel and equipment remained. But what is also certain is that part of the equipment and the manpower left and went to Yugoslavia, especially the part of the air force, the larger planes. That's what I can say as well even a layman, just a citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now move to another topic. The military command, except perhaps in a military dictatorship, received instructions from political authorities. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The military command receives instructions from the competent authorised command at the highest level; the superior command or Supreme Command. And I didn't hear of an insight into the Supreme Command to know if any influences was wielded on it. But the instructions, orders, came down to us from our superiors; from the superior command to the subordinate command. And reports went back from the subordinate command up towards the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true that there was a hierarchy within the military command, but it's not true, as you stated this morning on page 18 of the transcript, that the army was completely autonomous and independent. The army works on behalf of the political structures; does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The army executes the tasks and orders of the superior command. I was never able to see a document involving a political party or whether a political party or the president of a municipality or Executive Board or anything of that kind issue orders to the army, telling the army what it should do. I've never seen a document of that kind. I've never held one in my hands, nor did anybody issue any orders to me orally. And I don't know that others received orders from those sources either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the documents in a moment, Doctor. It's important for military and civilians to cooperate at all levels. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: If we're talking about health, the medical department, the medical corps, of course we did cooperate because it would be impossible to take some injured or sick person somewhere without contacting people from the civilian medical institutions. So in that sense, there would be a certain amount of cooperation. And so in that sense, we did cooperate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other units besides the medical corps, it's important for them to cooperate with the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, you ought to ask people from those structures that. If we're talking about a quartermaster service or something like that, the services generally did have to cooperate in one way or another in order to be able to reach certain areas, reach certain facilities, come by certain equipment. So that would be logical in that sense. Now, whether they cooperated in the sense of joint operation or implementing an order of any kind, I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I think it was General Talic, but once again, I can't say for sure. Before him, it was General Uzelac. Now whether it was General Talic, whether he had replaced him, I don't know but that's what I can tell you on that score.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit S346.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you read that document to yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you read that document to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Usher, here are copies of the document for the Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. In part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a document dated the 21st of May, 1992, from the commander, Major-General Momir Talic, sent to the commander chief of staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it deals with the general mobilisation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and it's an order. Can I ask you to read paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Immediately establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground offering expert and materiel support for the mobilisation process."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you also read paragraph 8(iv).

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Establish the closest possible cooperation with the people and legal authorities within their zones of responsibility. Before sending individuals or units into combat operations, always organise at least one session of target practice at an improvised firing range. Prepare small-scale combat operations to start with to ensure a degree of success in the first combat operation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So General Talic, who was the commander of the corps of which you were a member, obviously thinks it's important to have military and civilian cooperation, does he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes. Cooperation, and most probably when it says "municipal" here, they mean the departments for National Defence, and they were in charge of the mobilisation process. And it is these departments in the Ministry of Defence which were located on the territory of the municipality itself. I apologise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]..."immediately establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground." You're just reading into that that they are referring to departments of the National Defence. Sir, can you look at paragraph 6, please, and can you read it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "6. Explain to conscripts as they arrive the goals of our struggle and brief them on their duties and rights. Do not enlist any hesitant persons or suspicious persons into the units."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is referring to political objectives, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, you can interpret it that way, but I said this morning, and I claim again here and now, that the command never issued orders to civilian authorities, nor did the process take place vice versa. But when a unit spent some time in a certain area, it received commands from within the army. And as they were on the territory of a given municipality, there had to be some form of cooperation, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Cooperation between the military and the defence. Can you go to the distribution on the last page of the document. And it states there that as part of the distribution was the Prijedor Regional Command. Does it also list your unit, the 5th Medical Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Doctor, you testified earlier this morning - at page 25 of the transcript - that before the war, during the war, or after the war, it was not possible that the president of a municipality would issue orders to the medical corps or the president of the Executive Board or the president of the Crisis Staff of a municipality. You said there was absolutely no such possibility. You've also mentioned a number of times that you weren't aware of any documents. Was it possible to issue orders, decisions, and conclusions -- I'm sorry. I'll start that again: Was it possible for the municipal authorities, either a president of a municipality, a president of an Executive Board, or the president of the Crisis Staff, to issue orders, decisions, and conclusions to other units of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Within the medical corps that I'm talking about, and the medical battalion, I didn't see such a document, and I was not aware that either us or our command were issued any orders by any civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you some -- a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit S116.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware, though, of other units receiving orders, conclusions, or decisions from the municipal authorities, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I was not a member of any of these units; how could I know it? Only if I showed any interest before anybody, and if that person told me something. But I didn't hear any such stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't in a position to know. Sir, if you could read that document, and let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to present on the ELMO the English version in a way that we also can read the end of the document. A little bit further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise we don't have copies of this document before you. I spoke too soon. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you finished that document, reading that document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't that -- this is a document, Exhibit S116, is a summary of conclusions adopted by the Prijedor Municipality executive committee, relating to the public security service and regional command from 29 April to 17 August, 1992. Within that document, there are a number of decisions, orders, and conclusions which deal directly -- which directly involve military issues, are there not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time, and I already said that I wasn't there all the time. And thirdly, this is not an order. This is just an overview of conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff, for which I already said that I don't know who they were, what their role was in terms of command. We don't have a single order - and here I'm speaking on behalf of the medical corps - from the Crisis Staff, any order to carry out within the medical unit. I really don't have any such order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take you to conclusion number 02-111-171/92. Isn't that a conclusion of the Prijedor Municipality executive committee, assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command? It's dated the 10th of June, 1992. If I can take you to another one. The order number 02-111-315 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it's not possible to follow this way. If the number in front of the paragraph could be shown because we don't know where this number is. The page number and the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's far more easy -- the page number may be confusing, but the paragraphs are numbered. If you could make reference to the paragraphs as such, it would facilitate, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you start with the first summary or the second summary --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, the first one was dated the 10th of June, and it was conclusion number 171. And I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's start in the order, as we can see it on the English version, the second summary, orders from 29 May to 24 July. I think you're making reference to this only. And please then indicate whether you want to comment or put questions to the witness on paragraph 1, 2, or whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. I think I have the wrong exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Madam Registrar to crosscheck whether S116, as we have it before us, was previously 65 ter number 298.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Karper is checking the ERN number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, your results, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is 65 ter 298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then, I think as to the fact that there are several summaries, let's go through the entire document summary by summary. Do you want to make reference to the first summary of conclusions from 29 April to 17 August?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you just give me a moment, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour. And I apologise to the witness. Could the witness be shown Exhibit S250. And we will come back to Exhibit S116 in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we be shown the document first before it's shown to the witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Doctor, that is a rather lengthy document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. We don't have the English version on the ELMO, and we should also be able to follow. Okay. Please proceed. And I take it this is now the previously admitted Exhibit S250A on the ELMO, and B before the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this document is dated sometime in late July 1992. The date seems to be the 24th, or it could be another date. In any event, it's addressed to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and the subject is "Confirmation of decisions within the competence of the Municipal Assembly adopted by the Crisis Staff." And this document contains or lists a number of decisions, conclusions, and orders issued by the Prijedor Crisis Staff between the 29th of May and the 24th of July, 1992. If I can take you to the conclusion passed on the 10th of June which, for the usher's benefit, is under part 9, and conclusion number 2, which is the conclusion I referred you to earlier in the wrong document. And that is 02-111-171/92. That's a conclusion assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command. I now want to take you to another order issued on the 17th of June, 1992. And for the usher's benefit, that's under part number 13. And order number 1, which is 02-111-215/92, is an order for the formation of a single intervention platoon. If I can take you to order number 4 that's listed there, which is order number 02-111-218/92, that is an order concerning the obligation to report on the procurement of military equipment. If I can take you to a conclusion passed on the 23rd of June. For the usher's benefit, that's under part number 14, conclusion number 6, which is numbered 01-111-241/92, that's a conclusion directed to the regional command to ensure uniformity of the Serbian army insignia. Does this document show you that there were a number of conclusions, decisions, and orders sent from the Prijedor Crisis Staff to the regional command and others concerning military matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: You have provided me with too much material, too many facts. So I find it difficult to find my way around all this. I would like you to ask me question and read out one order which relates not to a proposal of conclusions but an order sent to the corps command or the command of a military active unit. For example, the 143rd or any other unit, because like this, I just can't find my way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I've just read you four conclusions and orders out of that document which directly involve military issues. And these are orders and conclusions issued by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Will you give me the exact number and page of what you just said, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Take your time, and let's do it step by step.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 6 in the document in your language -- have you got page 6?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I have page 6, and I'm reading it. But I'd like to ask you to tell me, please, what point you are referring to on this page. What does your question refer to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can go to part 9, enactments passed on the 10th of June, 1992. And the second -- paragraph 2 is the conclusion 171 that we have referred to above. That states there that it's assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command. This is a conclusion issued by the Prijedor Crisis Staff. So the Prijedor Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, this -- this is a political document and a conclusion. It is not an order, so we don't seem to be understanding each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conclusion is assigning the duty of providing security to the Trnopolje camp to the regional command, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The difference, in my opinion, is this - although I'm not a lawyer, I'm not well-versed in those things - but there's a big difference between conclusion and order. A conclusion doesn't imply implementation, execution. I don't see the consequences if this is not put into practice, whereas an order does; an order must be carried out. So in that sense, I cannot agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they are still telling the regional command what to do. They are telling the regional command to provide the security.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As a suggestion, as a proposal. But not as an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on. You wanted me to take you specifically to these conclusions and orders. The next one I mentioned was order number 215. You will find that on page 8 in the document in your language. And that is under -- that is number 18, right at the bottom of the page, under part number 13.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is an order concerning the formation of a single intervention platoon. Now, you just said a moment ago there was a difference between conclusions and orders.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In this order, I do not see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this order, the Prijedor Crisis Staff is ordering the formation of a single intervention platoon. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: What it says here is correct, but it is not correct that in an active-military unit of the army of Republika Srpska, the Crisis Staff issued orders to form an intervention platoon. I don't know that that was ever so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown this document. And it could be marked provisionally S3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 92. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But first, please, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is S391, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at that document and read it. It is somewhat illegible, parts of it are somewhat illegible. And if the English translation could be placed on the ELMO. For your benefit, I will read the document in full, because as I said, parts of it are illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are not clear how the date could be translated as well because it's not visible on this document, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Karper is requesting the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The best possible copy or original or whatsoever. We can read "datum 17." And then it's left for a guessing game. But I think we can see from the number that it's a number dated of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document -- this -- no, I take that back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the document is headed "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff. Number 02-111-215/92. Date: 17 June 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And at this point in time, we have to add that the witness has before himself a copy where one evidently can't read the month. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 3 and 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality at its meeting of 17 June 1992, the Prijedor Crisis Staff discussed the report on the security situation in the area of the municipality and issued the following order: "1. The Prijedor public security station and the Prijedor regional command are ordered to form a joint intervention squad within two days and each of them is to assign 20 members to the squad. Its main task should be the prevention of looting and other criminal activities in the area of the municipality, as well as of the movements of all unregistered vehicles and vehicles driven by the army and police members who are not in possession of properly authorised travel orders. "2. Squad members are to be selected from the existing ranks of the army and the police by the regional command and the public security station. "3. The Municipal Crisis Staff is to give approval for the selected squad members. "4. The regional command and the public security station are obliged to submit a report about the activities of the intervention squad and their results to the Municipal Crisis Staff within seven days. "5. This order takes effect on the day of its issuance." The signature block on the document is President of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic, Prijedor Municipal Assembly -- I'm sorry, that's the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we go -- enter into a dispute on this, I think we should agree that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just finish reading the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, there was an intervention, and therefore it's just fair --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to answer this objection. And I think it follows that apparently it's only typed, "Dr. Milomir Stakic," and then we have the same signature we had several times, but it reads "Za." And maybe the witness can or cannot of assistance to identify the signature. And then we have only in a legible form the left-hand side where we can read "Copies to."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Copies to, 1, public security station; 2, Prijedor regional command; and 3, files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, doesn't this document -- you wanted to see the actual order. Doesn't this document show you that the Prijedor Crisis Staff ordered the SJB and the Prijedor regional command to form a joint intervention squad within two days? So the Prijedor Crisis Staff are ordering the regional command to do something, the military.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that at that time, I was living in Banja Luka, and I don't know about the military institution -- a military institution which was called the regional command. I know that before the war, there was a garrison command or something of that kind in Prijedor. So I don't know -- of course I can't claim that it didn't exist, but I don't know this regional command. And secondly, this is quite certainly something that is outside the law on control and command in the army. And I'm -- whenever I say anything, I refer to that law, the law that made it impossible for an order to be received from civilian authorities and to be effective over the army. So this is not something that I knew happened, or happened frequently, and that these orders were exercised, implemented. And I must say quite frankly and honestly before this Tribunal that that is what I know and as far as I know. And that is what I base my claims on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That you weren't in the Prijedor Municipality at the time; you were in Banja Luka. And therefore, you don't know what was happening between the military and the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I don't know specific cases and events. I don't know about this particular event either. But on the basis of the military knowledge that I do have, working in the medical corps and what I was able to learn from the medical corps about the army as a whole, I claim and state that it was not possible, according to the provisions and the laws, for the civilian authorities to issue any orders to the army or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of this order then says: "Once the squad members have been selected, that the municipal Crisis Staff has to give their approval."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It reads on the transcript that your answer is not audible. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number three, you say. Point three of this order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is the same as to the previous question: I have no knowledge and am not aware of a document of this kind, and to the best of my knowledge and on the basis of what I know within the medical corps and outside the medical corps, there was never a situation of this kind, that is to say, in which we would receive orders from a civilian authority and were required to carry those orders out. That is to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections, or may I first ask the -- before we discuss this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. Can we get the best possible original in the course of this afternoon's hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We believe so, Your Honour. We haven't had a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us postpone the decision on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document has already been admitted as S79.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we would like to see the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Step by step, please. May I ask Madam Registrar, please, to crosscheck whether it's in fact the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S version has a different ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I then ask Ms. Karper to find out, we had a collection of the best possible originals or copies, and some in colour copies. If we could have the best possible one, the best readable one. Thank you. Here we are. And this is, in fact, S79. We have it before us, and may it first be shown... From our point of view, it's apparently an identical copy of the same document. May this document first be shown to the Defence, then to the Prosecution, and then to the witness, please. Based on this, all the problems we had in the past will immediately be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will cancel the request for the original of the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for the purpose of clarification, it clearly reads the 17th of June 1992 in the beginning. At the same time, also for clarification, the name Dr. Milomir Stakic is found on the document only in a typed version, and then we have this typical "Za" with any additional signature. May I ask the witness, did you ever come across with this signature? Do you know who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the first time I see this document and, obviously, the signature on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we withdraw that this document is provisionally marked as S391, because apparently the better and best possible version is the already-admitted Exhibit S79.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, as you've said, all you know is what is supposed to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, as you've said, all you know is what is supposed to happen; you don't know what actually happened because you weren't in a position to know. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "what happened"? What are you referring to when you say "you don't know what happened"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What actually happened between the civilian authorities and the military in the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Based on the documents that you have just shown me and my first-hand knowledge, it is obvious that I didn't know what was happening, the conflicts. The fact is, and I continue claiming that, that we didn't have any orders that we would carry out, and the medical corps was partly covering Prijedor as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see any orders.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before you move to another topic, I think it's appropriate to have a break now. Or is there a question following?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, are you aware of a policy to remove non-Serb officers in positions of authority from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such thing. And to be honest, I really did not pursue politics while I was in the army. And officers, for that matter, could not pursue politics or engage in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown a document, please, dated the 7th of June, 1992. The ERN number in B/C/S is 00423657. The Defence have been provided with a copy of this document. If that could be provisionally marked S391, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you read that document and advise me when you have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. While the witness is reviewing the document, can we have the 65 ter number for the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no Rule 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it should be reflected on the transcript that the ERN number is 03031763, the English version; and the B/C/S version, 00423657 and the following page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have had a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, this is dated the 7th of June 1992, Sanski Most. And it's conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting of political representatives of the municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc. And it was sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka, the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Could you please read aloud paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "We demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, and particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats. We believe that they cannot fight against their own people and that they are now involved in intelligence and other activities in the 1st Krajina Corps that are of interest to Ustasha forces and members of the so-called Alija's Territorial Defence. Deadline for completion: Seven days."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at another document, and then I will ask you some questions in relation to these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order that we don't forget, what about objections by the Defence related to the document provisionally marked S391?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to the authenticity, because there is no signature at all, but we will ask this witness several questions regarding this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore, as we did it previously, this document will be admitted into evidence as S391A for the English version and B for the B/C/S version. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just before we move off that document, there are seven conclusions stated in that document, and there is a stamp at the bottom of the document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's for the parties and for the members of the Bench to evaluate this. Thank you. You want to continue with the new document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, if that could be marked provisionally S392. And that's a document dated the 9th of June, Your Honour, and the ERN number in the B/C/S version is 00949887, and the English translation is 01105469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No 65 ter number for this case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that is a document dated the 9th of June, 1992, from the assistant commander for morale -- for moral guidance and legal affairs, Colonel Milutin Vukelic from the 1st Krajina Corps, and it's a report on the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff decision, and it's submitted to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army main staff and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency. Could you please read the document aloud.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Decision of the Crisis Staff of the Krajina Autonomous Region to the main staff of the army and the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "At yesterday's session of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, one of the issues that was discussed was the general personnel policy in the army and the 1st Krajina Corps. "It was stated that within the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, 14th logistics base, and the units of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence in Banja Luka garrison, there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croat nationality. An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by 15 June 1992, or they will take over the control of the armed forces. We consider their demand to be justified, but it is impossible to find adequate professional replacements among the reserve staff, and active officers of Bosnia-Herzegovina origin are not arriving from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Such action would also significantly weaken above-named units from which it has been requested that staff be purged. We are aware of a certain degree of danger, and we are excluding such persons from the more important decision-making processes. Our recommendation is to accelerate the process of sending active soldiers of BH origin over from FR Yugoslavia. The 1st Krajina Corps command should make the decision as to which staff members from the ranks of Muslims and Croats may still be temporarily kept and at what posts. "It would also be essential to take a position on what should be done with those who have not demonstrated any hostile activity so far, but who must be removed from key posts. "Milutin Vukelic, Colonel, assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document that we looked at, S391, shows that the civilian authorities in the subregional group of municipalities were requesting the Crisis Staff to cleanse the army of non-Serbs. The second document, the one we have just looked at, S392, then also discusses the issue that was discussed at the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, talking about purging staff from the 1st Krajina Corps, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I still maintain that this is a political document, so it was a request of the politics for things to be done in the army. The army responds in the way it did, but the army was never part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina or any other municipality territory, so they could not issue orders to the army. Obviously, nobody could forbid anybody to deliver such documents, and given the fact that this document indeed arrived, that could not have been forbidden. And they reacted as they did. And I continue maintaining the same position that, as far as I know, the politicians did try to realise their interests via the army. Whether they succeeded or not, and whether they had the legal right to do so or not, it is up to others to establish. I am not in the position to be familiar with that matter. I do not know the documents of this time dating back to that period. And therefore, I'm not in a position to say anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, in theory is one thing, and in practice is another.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In medical science, practice is sometimes stronger than its theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next document, which could be provisionally marked S -- we want to deal with the last document, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we reserve our right on this document, Your Honour? Because it says that it is done under cipher, and it seems that it's typed. So it's not clear whether it's -- on top. It said that it's coded and to be delivered immediately, but it doesn't seem, as the next document, you would see how it came through the machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, to the best of my recollection, we had already several documents that were, where we could read "coded." And we had already one expert on telecommunication. And emanating from this, I want to come back to our general decision from March or April 2002, admitting into evidence means, first of all, that the witness has testified. It was part of the hearing. And that we can come back and later on decide on the probative value of this document. Therefore, admitted into evidence as S392A, B respectively. And I'll emphasise on the same document, it is always possible if good reason will be shown that we reconsider this decision and may even quash our decision. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown the final document, provisionally if it could be marked S393. The B/C/S ERN number is 00820950, and the English translation is 03001521. And the document is dated the 9th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I am not able to provisionally mark this document because I don't know what it's all about. We have in B/C/S one typed document and one in handwriting. So before marking this document, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think the English translation is to 00820950, and the page that's attached to it I will leave for the moment, and that is 00820951.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 9th of June, 1992, which is the same date as the previous exhibit we just looked at. And it's sent from the commander of the army of the Serbian Republic, Colonel General Ratko Mladic. It is sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in relation to their reference, Document strictly confidential number 488-3 of the 9th of June, 1992, which is a reference to Exhibit S392. Could you please read the next paragraph aloud.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: To the "Command of the 1st Krajina Corps. Officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality must be sent on leave immediately. Take action at once to refer them to the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to resolve their status in the service."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The three exhibits that you have just read, S391, S392, and S393 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's not yet an S393. May I ask you also to have a look on the following page in handwriting. Maybe you, as a doctor, well acquainted with illegible handwriting, can see what is written on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's difficult, I must say. It's not only doctors who have this kind of handwriting. I do apologise, but I'm afraid I cannot read this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So for this reason, wouldn't it be appropriate to withdraw the handwritten document, because it also already reads in the English version that this page apparently is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I apologise for not making myself clearer. A moment ago I said I would leave that page and I was only seeking to tender the typewritten translation and the B/C/S ERN number 00820950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the objections by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for clarification, is there also no 65 ter number for this document as well, just so that we're clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct. And I have also been advised that 00820951 is actually on the back of the original document. But that text hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And apparently, it's not possible either to read or then to translate it. So therefore, we discuss only the two documents before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the same document, Your Honour, we would object to the authenticity of the document as well as the signature. But I would like to add in sum and substance, briefly, that with respect to the three documents, the Defence is contemplating filing a separate application in connection with those documents that we will bring in written form to the Court next week. So we explicitly and expressly reserve our right to do so since the Court has also said that these documents are provisionally marked, but I just wanted the record to be clear on that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be extremely concrete, in the moment, this document is provisionally marked 393. I've heard your objections. I told you that no doubt your right to challenge the decision later on, if you demonstrate reasons for this. But for the moment, as to the fact that the witness has testified based on this, this document is admitted into evidence as S393A and B respectively. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that's both the B/C/S pages -- Your Honour, just to be clear, the B/C/S includes the two pages, because the handwritten page is actually on the back of the typewritten page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can't proceed this way. In case the Prosecution finds a possibility to find a person who can read this document, then no doubt we can admit this into evidence, but just illegible parts of a document can't be admitted into evidence, even though we are aware, and it's reflected on the transcript, that apparently on the back side of Document S393B, it is your submission that there is something to be found in handwriting, and it's for you to find out whether we can read it later and to provide us with the entire original and the best possible original to be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to do that really more for completeness than anything, but we will get the original from the vault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, the three documents that you've just read, isn't it clear from that that the civilian authorities in the group of the -- the subregional group of municipalities sent a request on the 7th of June, 1992, to the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff and the leadership of the Serb Republic, requesting them to cleanse from the corps Muslims and Croats? Two days later, the 1st Krajina Corps then sends a document to the main staff, inter alia, stating that although they agreed with the instruction, it would be difficult to implement, and they were seeking guidance, instruction from the Autonomous Region Crisis Staff. And then on the same day, you have the order signed by Ratko Mladic that all superiors of Muslim and Croat nationality were to be sent on leave immediately and action was to be taken to refer them to the army of the FRY where their status would be resolved. And so this document makes it clear that the political figures do have their policies implemented.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, political figures did try, like in any other society and during the war as well, to influence certain events. Where they succeeded, where politics succeeded, well, these were acts. But this is a military order, and I can say that I have never seen this document before. This is the first time. So to me, as a physician, what this document contains, and the political request made differs greatly. There is a great difference between the two. And it is up to the Trial Chamber and others to assess and evaluate the reactions of the commander and the response by the command with respect to the requests made and the influence and efforts made to exert influence on the part of the political figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those documents show that the policy to remove non-Serb officers of -- non-Serb officers in positions of authority from the VRS is based purely on ethnic grounds. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: If you were to ask me not as an officer but as a man and a doctor if some of these officers, whether they were Muslims or Croats, if they were really temporarily removed from the war zone in Yugoslavia - and there were cases of that kind - and if they lived there and retired there, then I'm thinking, as an ordinary man, that would be a much better thing than some crimes perpetrated against them. And that was also something that happened. So I think that we should assess that in this light. I do not consider, however, that politics should have reacted in this way, which triggered off another reaction. But I leave it to the Court and others to decide what was to be done and how else this problem could have been solved in that general euphoria of war in which various cliques and ethnic groups wielded their influence, in which all partisan sides were seeking to wield their influence, different policies and politics. And so this is food for thought. We can think about this order in greater depth, the order issued by General Mladic, and place it in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that your answer to my question was yes, that these documents show that the policy to remove non-Serb officers in positions of authority from the VRS was based purely on ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, these people were not to say removed, but certain command duties, the men were replaced with persons that were not Muslim or other ethnic groups, that maybe they were not up to the task and duties imposed upon them. So that I really can't say that I agree with you, and that that was -- that the reason for their removal was ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, the first document dated the 7th of June clearly is a request to cleanse the corps from Muslims and Croats. The second document, dated the 9th of June, talks about a decision to replace 67 non-Serb officers. Mladic's decision clearly, dated the 9th of June, the same as the previous document, states that all superiors of Muslim and Croat nationality were to be sent on leave. My question again: These three documents clearly show that the policy to remove officers was based on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the question was already answered by the witness on page 80, line 10, following when he stated that it would be better "if they were really temporarily removed from the war zone in Yugoslavia - and there were cases of that kind - and if they lived there and retired there, then I'm thinking as an ordinary man, that would be a much better thing than some crimes perpetrated against them." And from this, I take that you have experienced examples that crimes were committed against those persons. Correct? Please answer, that it's reflected on the transcript, not only nodding. Could you please be so kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We learned this morning that after your graduation, you started working in Prijedor on or about 1979. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's extremely difficult to work with the correct terms in this Tribunal because the terminology is different. In one country, you use this term; in another country, that term. Therefore, my question would be: Whom did you regard as the political leader of Prijedor in general?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In 1979, when I started working in Prijedor, there was a one-party, single-party system, and that was communism. The communist party. And we knew where the leadership lay, and we knew who was at the head of communism. We were united in that sense. And my leader at that time was Tito.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wasn't there a, let's call it, subleader in the area of Prijedor already at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: You're asking me about 1979, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The old politicians of the day, dating back to those times; Drasko Popovic, Nikola Stojanovic to name a few. Younger politicians of my own age, I don't remember those. I don't remember any younger politicians whom I could refer to as being my political leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's go immediately one step further: 1990, 1991, who was at that time the political leader in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In 1990, as far as I recall, there were general elections. And in Prijedor, the party that won the elections with a slight majority was the SDA. That is to say, the Muslim party. But according to some of the electoral results, this was almost equal to the SDS party, whereas the Croatian party received far fewer votes. So that I personally in the sense of leadership, a political leader, I can't actually remember anybody that stood out as a political leader. And as I say, at that time, I was living in Banja Luka, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you by chance, even though I know that you lived in Banja Luka, knew Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Cehajic's wife very well. She was Dr. Milka. And she taught me, because I spent the first days of my internship working under her. She was a very good professional, very good doctor, and a humanist. I didn't know him personally, although I heard about him through her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever, after 1992, have a meeting with Madam Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know about the fate of the late Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it. I heard that -- I heard what had happened to him in 1992, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And do you know the reasons why this happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know the details of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Dr. Stakic after 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I think we met, as I said earlier on, sometime in 1994 in the Presidency, or rather at the meetings of the physicians -- the society of physicians of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you at that time also discuss political issues?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember discussing political issues. We discussed our own society, our own association, because we felt the need for the society to function, to actually be active in all regions, not just to exist as dead letter on paper, so in the municipalities, and our discussions went along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to present to the witness Document D50B. Was there at that time a Minister of Defence? And where in this hierarchy would you allocate the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, on the first rung of the ladder, in the supreme council, the Defence Minister is on that body. And by virtue of office, he should take part in the Supreme Command as well. But as far as I know, the Supreme Commander is independent and autonomous in making decisions. And usually, it is embodied in the person of the president of the Republic, president of the country, state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So would it be correct to put the Minister of Defence in box 1 of your own sketch?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Well, he should be there. But I really don't know exactly whether he would be or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some minutes ago, you stated that you are not aware of the notion of a Prijedor regional command and referred, to the best of your recollection, to Prijedor garrison command. Where in this hierarchy would we find the Prijedor garrison command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: In number 6. No, I apologise. Number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please explain for us, having not served in the military, what is your understanding of a garrison command? How many persons are there? Who is the leader of such a garrison command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The garrison command is an institution which should technically, in the sense of manpower, serve the active component in the town, that is to say, military pensioners. It should authorise and authenticate health documents. And there's usually an army club attached to the garrison, where cultural events take place in the military sense. But I'm talking about peacetime. In times of war -- that's why I say that was how it was before the war. Now, after the war, a brigade was set up, the 143rd Brigade. Now, whether that command was within the brigade composition or not, or whether it was the regional command of Prijedor was something else again. I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know anybody in person in the Prijedor garrison command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: I knew Dr. Zeljko Macura, who was a doctor there, and he was chief of the medical corps. He was not an active-duty serviceman. I remember him from the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Arsic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of Mr. Arsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And would he be part of this Prijedor garrison command, or even the commander of this garrison command? Sorry for asking you these questions on ranks in the military hierarchy, but we really need to know this.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: For a while, he was the commander of the 143rd. Whether he was -- I've already told you that I'm not familiar with the fact whether the command was in the composition of the unit. So I don't know whether he was in the garrison command and in the regional command in the way this is mentioned in the document. But I know that he was in that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Whom would you regard as your colleague or subordinate on the level of Prijedor, responsible for taking care of all the health problems of this garrison command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: It was Dr. Macura. I cooperated with him, and he was in that unit. That was one of the largest units in Prijedor, although it was not in the composition of the Prijedor area. Its manpower was from other municipalities; from Novi Grad, Sanski Most, and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Macura ever report to you on certain problems emanating from the number of wounded persons caused by incidents, be it in Prijedor, be it in Kozarac, be it in Hambarine, be it Omarska, be it in Keraterm, or wheresoever? Was this once an issue that he felt necessary to report to you, that they had enormous problems?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. In the corps command, there was also a chief of the command corps of that corps. It was Colonel Dikic, Branko Dikic. All the reports on medical issues from all the units, including the medical corps of Dr. Macura, arrived at the desk of the chief of medical corps in the 1st Corps, and in my medical battalion, which was a stationary institution, and it was not an operational unit in the same sense as the medical units in the brigade and lower-ranking units. That is where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Before I turn to a number of documents, isn't it true that in wartimes, in extraordinary times, it was necessary that those powers, normally divided for good reason, had to cooperate more closely than in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. But when it came to medical issues and medical corps, we cooperated because we had to do that. We had to cooperate in our work. We couldn't treat all the wounded and sick only in our institution. We had to rely on civilian institutions, and we had to cooperate in our profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to present to the witness Document S180B. And could you please start with page number 76, item number 115. May I ask in the meantime, did you ever read Official Gazettes, or was this more or less boring for you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Mostly boring. Only when I had to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please have a look on this document. And could you please read out item number 115.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Should I read it this aloud? "It is hereby suggested to the regional command of Prijedor that in cooperation with the" -- this is something I can't see too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It starts on the top of the page 115.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 3 and Article 70 -" I can't read the second number - "of the decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor Municipality, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality at its session held on the 23rd of June, 1992, issues the following conclusion: It is hereby suggested that the regional command of Prijedor should, in cooperation with the higher command, coordinate and regulate the unique insignia of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Second, this conclusion shall come into effect on the day of its passing. President of the Crisis Staff, Milan Kovacevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Dr. Kovacevic, yes. I knew him from our university days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you hear also about his political career?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was the president of the Executive Board of Prijedor Municipality in 1992. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And now, to the contents of this conclusion, you made a clear distinction between conclusion and order, and we perfectly understood this. What is your understanding, that a Crisis Staff in Prijedor come to the conclusion to have unified insignia for the army? Could you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: My comment could be the following: Political structures and institutions tried to influence the unified insignia. Whether this was implemented, whether this was carried through, and whether this was according to military regulations, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So maybe it's helpful to come back to a more fundamental document. The same Official Gazette, the same exhibit number, S180, if you could please read out item number 18. This is on, English version, the second page, for the assistance of the usher. The decision that reads: "Decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff." Could you please be so kind and read out the first half part of Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "In the implementation of its function within the area of defence activities, the Crisis Staff will do the following things particularly: It will coordinate the work and activities of the participants in the general people's defence. It will consider the issues of mobilisation, development, and the replenishment of the armed forces and other structures, and initiate with other competent municipal bodies cooperation with the former structures based on --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This is enough. What's your comment on this in a decision taken by Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff discussing the reinforcement of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: The Official Gazette that I see in front of you, I never read before. That's first. And secondly, during the war, when I did my job, this is not something that I would think about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you then could proceed in the same document, item 18, Article 9, please. If you could be so kind and read aloud Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: "Crisis Staff maintains permanent coordination and cooperation with the army of the Serbian Republic -- Bosnian Republic. And it engages in the civilian protection via the officials and officers of these institutions and bodies through the Executive Board of the municipality and with all the other economic and social subjects in the area of the municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you for comments on this article. On the cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other organs.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR PUSAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this is a political platform of the Crisis Staff. But there's no single military document. And not just military documents, but instructions. I have not come across anything similar to this. I have not come across something like this that existed and was implemented in the military bodies and commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we then turn in the same Official Gazette, the same exhibit number, to item number 20. If you could read this aloud, please.
